events.title: The Shepherd in the Fields of Bethlehem
events.subtitle: In the fields where no one was watching
story: When the evening light settled over the hills of Bethlehem, the bleating of the flock scattered down the slopes. David, the youngest of Jesse's eight sons, kept his father's sheep in those fields. He was a ruddy boy with clear, bright eyes. While his older brothers took on the weighty matters of the household, the youngest one's place was always beside the flock.

One day a lion appeared, seized a lamb in its jaws and ran off. The boy did not hesitate. He chased after it, struck the beast, and pulled the lamb out of its mouth. When the lion turned and sprang at him, David caught it by the beard, struck it and killed it. When a bear came, he did the same.

There was no one in those fields to applaud. David only spoke of it years later, when he stood before King Saul and offered to fight a giant. This is what the boy told the king: “Your servant has been keeping his father's sheep. The Lord who rescued me from the claws of the lion and the bear will rescue me this time too.”

words.text: Your servant has been keeping his father's flock. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb, I went after it, struck it and rescued the lamb from its mouth.
The Lord who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine as well.
There is still the youngest. He is out in the fields right now, tending the sheep.

events.note: In David's day lions and bears still lived in the hill country of Judah. A shepherd carried a staff, a sling and a bag of food, and guarded his sheep from wild animals. Bethlehem is a hill village about ten kilometers south of Jerusalem.
events.reflect: Even where no one is watching, do I faithfully do the work I've been given?

quiz.q: Which animals did David fight and defeat while guarding the sheep?
quiz.explain: David told Saul that when a lion or a bear carried off a lamb, he went after it and rescued it, and that he had killed both lion and bear (1 Sam 17:34–36).

events.title: Oil Poured on Jesse's Youngest
events.subtitle: People look at the face, God looks at the heart
story: The old prophet Samuel had long been grieving over Saul, the king God had rejected. Then the Lord spoke to him: “How long will you go on grieving? Fill your horn with oil and go to Jesse of Bethlehem. I have chosen a king from among his sons.” Samuel answered, “If Saul hears of it, he will kill me.” The Lord said, “Take a heifer with you and say you have come to offer a sacrifice.”

When the prophet arrived, the elders of Bethlehem came out trembling. “Do you come in peace?” they asked. Samuel answered, “I do. I have come to offer a sacrifice.” When Jesse's eldest son Eliab stood before him, Samuel thought, “Surely this is the one.” But the Lord said, “Do not look at his face or his height. People look at the outside, but I look at the heart.”

Not Abinadab, and not Shammah either. When all seven sons had passed by, Samuel asked, “Are these all the sons you have?” Jesse answered, “The youngest is left, but he is out tending the sheep.” Samuel said no one would sit down until the boy arrived. When the boy called in from the fields walked through the door, the Lord said, “Get up and anoint him. This is the one.” The oil ran down before his brothers' eyes, and from that day on the Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon David.

words.text: Do not look at his face or his great height. I have not chosen him. People see what the eyes can see, but I, the Lord, see the heart.
Get up and anoint him. This is the one.
Send for the boy and bring him here. We will not sit down until he comes.

events.note: Anointing with oil was how God set a person apart as king or priest. In Hebrew, “the anointed one” is the Messiah. Saul too had earlier been anointed by Samuel.
events.reflect: Do I judge people only by their looks and their circumstances?

quiz.q: Which of Jesse's sons did Samuel first think was surely the one the Lord would anoint?
quiz.explain: Samuel thought so when he saw Eliab, the eldest, but the Lord told him not to look at his appearance or his height (1 Sam 16:6–7).

events.title: The Boy Who Played the Lyre
events.subtitle: The sound of a lyre in a darkened palace
story: The Spirit of the Lord had left Saul, and an evil spirit sent from the Lord tormented the king. A heavy shadow fell over the palace at Gibeah. His servants spoke up carefully: “Let us look for someone who plays the lyre well. When the evil spirit comes on you, he can play, and you will feel better.” Saul said, “Find me someone who plays well and bring him to me.”

One of the young attendants stepped forward. “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem. He plays the lyre well, he is a brave warrior, he speaks wisely and he is fine to look at. And the Lord is with him.” So Saul sent word to Jesse: “Send me your son David, the one who tends the sheep.” Jesse loaded a donkey with bread, a skin of wine and a young goat, and sent his son.

When Saul saw David he loved him dearly and made him his armor-bearer. Saul sent word to Jesse again: “Let David stay in my service. I am pleased with him.” From then on, whenever the evil spirit overwhelmed the king, the boy took up his lyre and plucked the strings. As the melody spread through the dark room, Saul could breathe again and grew better, and the evil spirit left him.

words.text: I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem. He plays the lyre well, he is brave, he speaks wisely and he is fine to look at. And the Lord is with him.
Find me someone who plays the lyre well and bring him to me.
Let David stay in my service. I am pleased with him.

events.note: The lyre, called the kinnor in Hebrew, was a small stringed instrument with strings stretched across a wooden frame and plucked by hand. Gibeah, where Saul's palace stood, is thought to be Tell el-Ful, north of Jerusalem.
events.reflect: Am I a small comfort to the weary people around me?

quiz.q: What role did Saul give David when he kept him at court?
quiz.explain: Saul loved David greatly and made him his armor-bearer (1 Sam 16:21).

events.title: The Giant in the Valley of Elah
events.subtitle: Forty days of a giant's taunts
story: With the Valley of Elah between them, Israel camped on one hill and the Philistines on the other. Every day one man walked out of the Philistine camp: Goliath of Gath. He stood six cubits and a span tall, and his bronze helmet and coat of scale armor weighed five thousand shekels. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his shield-bearer walked ahead of him.

The giant shouted across the valley: “Choose one of your men and send him down to me. If he kills me, we will be your slaves. If I kill him, you will be our slaves.” All Israel trembled, and Saul promised great wealth, his own daughter, and freedom from taxes for his father's house to the man who killed him. Morning and evening, it went on like that for forty days.

David was still going back and forth between Saul's court and his father's sheep in Bethlehem, and around that time Jesse sent his youngest to his brothers with roasted grain and ten loaves of bread. As soon as David reached the camp, the giant's taunts rang in his ears. The soldiers shrank back in fear, but the boy asked the men standing near him, “Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” His eldest brother Eliab heard and flared up: “Who did you leave those few sheep with?”

words.text: Who is this uncircumcised Philistine anyway, that he dares to defy the armies of the living God?
What have I done now? I only asked a question.
Today I defy the armies of Israel. Send out a man, and let the two of us fight it out.
Why have you come down here? Who did you leave those few sheep with out in the wilderness? You only came to watch the battle.

events.note: Six cubits and a span is about 2.9 meters. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read four cubits and a span, a little over 2 meters. The Valley of Elah was the route that climbed from the Philistine plain into the hill country of Judah.
events.reflect: Facing a frightening problem, am I forgetting how great God is?

quiz.q: For how long did Goliath come out morning and evening to stand before the Israelite camp?
quiz.explain: The Philistine came forward morning and evening for forty days (1 Sam 17:16).

events.title: Five Smooth Stones
events.subtitle: Not with a sword, but in the name of the Lord
story: David came before Saul and said, “Your servant will go and fight this Philistine.” Saul tried to stop him: “You are only a boy, and he has been a warrior since his youth.” David answered, “The Lord who rescued me from the lion and the bear will rescue me again.” Saul dressed him in his own tunic and put a bronze helmet on his head. David took a few steps and said, “I can't go in these. I'm not used to them.”

David took off the armor, went down to the stream, chose five smooth stones and put them in his shepherd's bag. In his hand, a single sling. The giant looked at the ruddy boy and despised him. Goliath shouted, “Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” David shouted back, “You come with a sword, a spear and a javelin, but I come in the name of the Lord of hosts. The battle belongs to the Lord.”

As the giant came closer, David ran toward him. He took a stone from his bag and slung it. The stone sank into his forehead, and the giant fell face down on the ground. There was no sword in David's hand. He ran over, drew the giant's sword from its sheath, and with it cut off Goliath's head. The Philistine army fled, and Israel chased them with a great shout to the gates of Gath and Ekron.

words.text: You come to me with a sword, a spear and a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.
The Lord does not save by sword or spear. This battle belongs to the Lord, and he will give you into our hands.
Go, and may the Lord be with you.
You come at me with sticks? Am I a dog?

events.note: A sling was a leather pouch with two cords. The slinger whirled it around and let go of one cord to send the stone flying. Judges 20:16 tells of Benjamite slingers who could hit a hair without missing. It was no shepherd's toy but a weapon of war.
events.reflect: Envying the way others do things, do I make light of what God has given me?

quiz.q: How many stones did David pick from the stream and put in his bag?
quiz.explain: David chose five smooth stones from the stream and put them in his shepherd's bag (1 Sam 17:40).

events.title: Jonathan's Covenant
events.subtitle: A friend he loved as his own life
story: The boy stood before Saul with the giant's head in his hand. Wanting to know which house should receive the promised reward, Saul asked, “Young man, whose son are you?” David answered, “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.” By the time that short answer was over, the prince Jonathan, who had been watching nearby, found his heart bound fast to David's. Jonathan loved him as his own life.

That day Saul took David and would not let him go back to his father's house. Jonathan made a covenant with David. He took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow and even his belt. One by one, the king's son handed what he had to a shepherd from the fields.

Wherever Saul sent him, David went and succeeded wisely. Saul set him over the soldiers. All the people thought well of him, and so did Saul's officials. In the palace at Gibeah, one the son of a king and the other the son of a shepherd, the two stood side by side within one covenant.

words.text: I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.
Young man, whose son are you?

events.note: In the ancient Near East, handing over one's robe and weapons was a sign of sharing one's own place and portion. Jonathan was the prince in line for the throne, and also the warrior who broke the Philistine camp at Michmash in 1 Samuel 14.
events.reflect: Can I truly bless someone who is getting ahead of me?

quiz.q: Which of these did Jonathan NOT give David?
quiz.explain: Jonathan gave David his robe and tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt (1 Sam 18:4).

events.title: Thousands and Tens of Thousands
events.subtitle: One line of a song changed the king's eyes
story: On the way home from fighting the Philistines, women came out of every town in Israel with tambourines, dancing and singing: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” The more they sang it, the harder the king's face became. Saul was furious. “They credit David with tens of thousands, and me with only thousands,” he said. “What more can he get but the kingdom?” From that day on Saul kept a suspicious eye on David.

The next day an evil spirit rushed upon Saul. The king raved inside the house, and David played the lyre as on any other day. Saul gripped the spear in his hand and said to himself, “I will pin David to the wall.” The spear flew, and twice David dodged it. Saul knew the Lord was with David and had left him, and he was afraid of David.

Saul made David a commander of a thousand and sent him out to battle. He promised him his daughter, while hoping David would fall at the hands of the Philistines. Saul's daughter Michal loved David. The bride price the king asked for was a hundred Philistine foreskins. Before the time was up, David went out and struck down two hundred. Michal became David's wife, and Saul remained David's enemy for the rest of his life.

words.text: Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?
Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.
They credit David with tens of thousands and me with only thousands. What more is left for him to get but the kingdom?

events.note: The bride price was a gift the groom paid to the bride's family; it appears also in Genesis 34 and Exodus 22. Instead of money, Saul demanded proof of a hundred dead Philistines, hoping David would fall in battle.
events.reflect: When I see someone else succeed, what is the first feeling that rises in my heart?

quiz.q: What bride price did Saul demand from David in return for Michal?
quiz.explain: Saul sent word that the king wanted no bride price but a hundred Philistine foreskins, and David struck down two hundred Philistines (1 Sam 18:25–27).

events.title: The Night He Went Down Through the Window
events.subtitle: The window Michal opened
story: Saul told his son Jonathan and his officials to kill David. Jonathan, who loved David dearly, warned him in secret: “Stay hidden until morning. I will speak to my father.” Standing before his father in the field, Jonathan said, “David risked his life to strike down the Philistine, and the Lord won a great victory for all Israel. Why would you shed innocent blood?”

Saul listened and swore an oath: “As surely as the Lord lives, he will not be put to death.” David came back to the king's side. But when David returned from another great victory over the Philistines, the evil spirit seized Saul again. Between the notes of the lyre, Saul's spear came flying. It stuck in the wall, and that night David slipped away.

Saul sent men to watch David's house, with orders to kill him when morning came. Michal told her husband, “If you don't get away tonight, tomorrow you will be dead.” She let David down through a window. Then she laid the household idol in the bed, put goat hair at its head and covered it with a garment. David slipped out between the men surrounding the house. Of that night David sang, “My God, rescue me from my enemies.”

words.text: My king, do not sin against your servant David. He took his life in his hands and struck down the Philistine, and the Lord brought about a great victory for all Israel.
As surely as the Lord lives, I swear it: he will not be put to death.
If you don't save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.
Why did you deceive me like this, and let my enemy go so that he escaped?

events.note: The teraphim were household idols; it was teraphim that Rachel stole from her father Laban's house. The heading of Psalm 59 says it was written when Saul sent men to watch David's house in order to kill him.
events.reflect: Can I bravely stand up for someone who has been treated unfairly?

quiz.q: After helping David escape, what did Michal lay in the bed?
quiz.explain: Michal laid the household idol in the bed, put a quilt of goat hair at its head and covered it with a garment (1 Sam 19:13).

events.title: The Prophets of Ramah
events.subtitle: The Spirit of God that even a king could not stop
story: Having escaped Saul's hand, David went to Samuel at Ramah. Before the old prophet who had anointed him, he poured out everything Saul had done. The two of them went to Naioth and stayed there. Soon someone reported it to Saul: “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”

Saul sent men to seize David. When they arrived, a company of prophets was prophesying, with Samuel standing at their head and leading them. The Spirit of God came upon Saul's men, and they too began to prophesy. Saul sent more men, and they prophesied as well. So did the third group he sent.

At last Saul went to Ramah himself. At the great well in Secu he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” On the road to Naioth the Spirit of God came upon Saul too. The king prophesied as he walked, and before Samuel he stripped off his robes and lay there unclothed all that day and night. People whispered, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

words.text: David is at Naioth in Ramah right now.
Where are Samuel and David?
Is Saul also among the prophets?

events.note: Naioth means “dwellings” and is thought to be the place in Ramah where a company of prophets lived together around Samuel. The saying “Is Saul also among the prophets?” had first come up after Saul was anointed (1 Samuel 10:11–12).
events.reflect: What have I tried to solve on my own instead of leaving it with God?

quiz.q: Before going himself, how many times did Saul send men to Naioth to seize David?
quiz.explain: All three groups of messengers Saul sent ended up prophesying, and then Saul went to Ramah himself (1 Sam 19:20–22).

img.title: Saul among the Prophets

events.title: Three Arrows
events.subtitle: The arrow of promise that flew beyond
story: Fleeing from Naioth, David asked Jonathan, “What have I done, that your father is after my life?” Jonathan answered, “It can't be. You will not die.” David shook his head. “There is only a step between me and death.” David decided to stay away from the New Moon feast and hide in the field. As they made a covenant, Jonathan said, “Never withdraw your kindness from my house.”

On the second day of the New Moon, David's place at the king's table was empty again. Saul asked, “Why hasn't the son of Jesse come, either yesterday or today?” When Jonathan gave the excuse they had agreed on, Saul exploded: “As long as the son of Jesse lives, neither you nor your kingdom will be established. He must die.” Jonathan stood up to him: “Why should he die?” Instead of an answer, Saul's spear flew at his own son.

The next morning Jonathan went out to the field with a young servant boy. An arrow flew over the boy's head. Jonathan called out, “Isn't the arrow beyond you? Hurry! Don't stop!” It was the signal for David, hidden behind the rock, to go. When the boy had gone back, David came out and bowed down to the ground three times. The two kissed each other and wept together, but David wept the most. Jonathan said, “Go in peace.”

words.text: As surely as the Lord lives and as you live, there is only a step between me and death.
Go in peace. The two of us have sworn in the name of the Lord, and the Lord will be between you and me, and between your descendants and mine, forever.
Show me the Lord's steadfast love as long as I live. And even after I die, never withdraw that love from my house.
As long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom will stand secure.

events.note: The New Moon was the day the new moon appeared, a festival with trumpets, offerings and a shared meal (Numbers 10:10; 28:11). Scripture calls the rock beside the place where David hid and waited the stone Ezel.
events.reflect: Even as a relationship grows distant, do I keep the promises I should keep?

quiz.q: How many arrows did Jonathan say he would shoot to let David know his father's intentions?
quiz.explain: Jonathan said he would shoot three arrows beside the rock as though shooting at a target (1 Sam 20:20). Saying the arrows were beyond the boy was the signal to leave (1 Sam 20:22).

events.title: The Holy Bread of Nob and Goliath's Sword
events.subtitle: Holy bread for a hungry fugitive, and what it cost
story: Having slipped away from Saul's court, David arrived empty-handed at the sanctuary of Nob. The priest Ahimelech came out trembling to meet him. “Why are you alone?” Ahimelech asked. “Is no one with you?” David made up a story: “The king has sent me on a secret errand. Just give me five loaves of bread.” There was nothing in the sanctuary but the holy bread that had just been removed. Ahimelech handed David the bread that had been replaced with fresh loaves before the Lord.

David asked again, “Is there a spear or a sword here? The king's business was so urgent I didn't even bring my sword.” Ahimelech answered, “The sword of Goliath, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, is here, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod.” David said, “There is none like it. Give it to me.” But someone else was there that day: Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul's shepherds. Doeg watched it all without a word.

Some time later Doeg reported to Saul what he had seen that day. At Saul's command, Doeg killed eighty-five priests. Only Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, escaped and ran to David. David said to Abiathar, “When I saw Doeg there that day, I knew this would happen. Your father's whole family is dead because of me. Stay with me. You are safe here.” Later David sang of Doeg, “Why do you boast of evil, you mighty man?”

words.text: When I saw Doeg the Edomite there that day, I knew he would surely tell Saul. The death of your father's whole family is on me.
Don't be afraid; stay with me. The one who is after your life is after mine too. With me you will be safe.
There is no sword like it anywhere. Give it to me.
Who among all your servants is as faithful as David? He is the king's son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard, and honored in your house.

events.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set out fresh each Sabbath on the table in the sanctuary, and the loaves that were removed could be eaten only by priests (Lev 24:5–9). Jesus pointed to this event in a dispute about the Sabbath (Mark 2:25–26).
events.reflect: Have words I blurted out in fear hurt someone else?

quiz.q: How many priests did Doeg kill at Nob?
quiz.explain: That day Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five priests who wore the linen ephod (1 Sam 22:18). Only Abiathar son of Ahimelech escaped and fled to David (1 Sam 22:20).

events.title: Feigning Madness in Gath
events.subtitle: A hero turned madman at the enemy's gate
story: David stood alone before the gate of Gath in the land of the Philistines, Goliath's hometown. In his flight from Saul he had run out of places to hide in Israel. Surely in the enemy's land Saul could not reach him. David went before Achish, king of Gath.

But Achish's servants recognized him first. They whispered to the king, “Isn't this David, the king of the land? The very man the women sang about as they danced: Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands?” Those words pierced David's heart. He became deeply afraid of Achish.

In front of them David suddenly became another man. He twisted his body, scratched marks all over the doors of the gate and let spit run down his beard. Achish shouted at his servants, “Look, the man is mad! Why bring him to me? Am I so short of madmen that you bring this one to rave in front of me?” And so David left Gath as good as driven out. Of that fearful day David sang, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.”

words.text: Isn't this David, the king of the land? Isn't he the one they danced and sang about: Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands?
Look, the man is mad! Why did you bring him to me? Am I so short of madmen that you bring this one into my house?

events.note: Gath was one of the five Philistine cities and Goliath's hometown (1 Sam 17:4). It is widely identified today with Tell es-Safi. The headings of Psalms 56 and 34 point to this event.
events.reflect: Instead of covering my fear with pretense, do I come to God honestly?

quiz.q: Which of these did David NOT do while feigning madness in Gath?
options: Scratched marks on the doors of the gate
Let spit run down his beard
quiz.explain: David changed his behavior before Achish, pretending to be mad, scratching on the doors of the gate and letting spit run down his beard (1 Sam 21:13). There is no record of him swinging a sword.

img.title: David Feigning Madness before Achish

events.title: Four Hundred in the Cave of Adullam
events.subtitle: A cave where the indebted and the bitter gathered
story: Barely escaped from Gath, David crept into the cave of Adullam at the foot of the hills of Judah. There was nothing there but darkness, except for the light seeping through the cracks in the rock. Then familiar faces appeared at the mouth of the cave. His brothers and his father's household had heard the news and come down.

And others came too: people on the run, people crushed by debt, people bitter in spirit. One by one they gathered, until there were about four hundred. David became their leader. His first army was not the warriors of a royal court but people the world had pushed aside.

David took his aged parents to Mizpah in Moab and asked the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay here until I know what God will do for me.” After that the prophet Gad told David, “Don't stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah.” David left for the forest of Hereth. In those days of hiding in the cave, David cried out, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.”

words.text: Please let my father and mother come and stay with you until I know what God will do for me.
Do not stay in this stronghold. Leave and go into the land of Judah.

events.note: Adullam was an ancient town in the Shephelah, the lowlands of Judah, whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:15). Some suggest David left his parents in Moab because his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite woman (Ruth 4:17).
events.reflect: How do I treat people who have been hurt and pushed aside?

quiz.q: About how many people gathered to David at the cave of Adullam?
quiz.explain: Everyone in distress, in debt or bitter in spirit gathered to David, about four hundred men, and he became their leader (1 Sam 22:2).

img.title: Landscape with David at the Cave of Adullam
img.credit: Claude Lorrain, Landscape with David at the Cave of Adullam, 1658 · National Gallery, London · Public domain

events.title: Rescuing Keilah
events.subtitle: When the town he saved was ready to shut its gates
story: News came that the Philistines were attacking Keilah and looting the grain from its threshing floors. David asked the Lord, “Shall I go and attack them?” The Lord answered, “Go, attack the Philistines and save Keilah.” But his men shook their heads: “Even hiding here in Judah we are afraid. And you want us to go all the way to Keilah to fight the Philistine army?”

David asked again. This time the Lord's answer was even clearer: “Get up and go down to Keilah. I will give the Philistines into your hand.” David and his men went down, struck the Philistines hard and carried off their livestock. The people of Keilah were saved. Around that time Abiathar, the priest who alone had survived at Nob, came to David bringing the ephod.

When Saul heard the news, he exclaimed with delight, “David has walked right into a town with gates and bars and shut himself in!” Before the ephod, David asked, “Will Saul come down?” The Lord answered, “He will come down.” David asked again, “Will the people of Keilah hand me over?” The Lord said, “They will hand you over.” David and his men, about six hundred of them, left Keilah and wandered wherever they could go. Saul called off the expedition.

words.text: Go, attack the Philistines and save Keilah.
Get up and go down to Keilah. I will give the Philistines into your hand.
Lord, God of Israel, your servant has clearly heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the town because of me.
They will hand you over.

events.note: Keilah was a town in the Shephelah south of Adullam, about 13 km northwest of Hebron, identified today with Khirbet Qila. Threshing floors lay outside the town walls, making them an easy target for raiders at harvest.
events.reflect: Can I do good even to someone who will not be grateful?

quiz.q: About how many men were with David when he left Keilah?
quiz.explain: David and his men, about six hundred, set out and left Keilah and went wherever they could go (1 Sam 23:13).

img.title: David Consults the High Priest through the Ephod

events.title: Betrayed in the Wilderness of Ziph
events.subtitle: Two friends in the wilderness, and a chase around a mountain
story: David moved from stronghold to stronghold in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not give David into his hands. Then Saul's son Jonathan came to find David at Horesh. Jonathan took David's hand and said, “Don't be afraid. My father's hand will not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you.” The two made a covenant before the Lord and parted. It was the last time they would meet.

But the Ziphites of that land went up to Gibeah and informed Saul: “Isn't David hiding among us, in the strongholds on the hill of Hachilah?” Saul blessed them and said, “You have had compassion on me. Go and find out every place where he hides.” Saul led his troops all the way down to the wilderness of Maon.

Saul went along one side of the mountain, David along the other. David hurried to get away, while Saul's men closed in around him. He was on the point of being caught. Just then a messenger ran up to Saul: “Come back quickly! The Philistines have raided the land.” Saul turned back. That is why the place was called Sela-hammahlekoth, the Rock of Parting. Of that day David sang, “Save me, O God, by your name.”

words.text: Don't be afraid. The hand of my father Saul will not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you.
Isn't David hiding among us, in the strongholds at Horesh on the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon?
May the Lord bless you, for you have had compassion on me.
Come back quickly! The Philistines have raided the land.

events.note: Ziph is identified with Tell Zif, about 7 km southeast of Hebron. East of it the parched wilderness of Judah stretches down to the Dead Sea. Horesh was the last place Jonathan and David met in this life.
events.reflect: Who can I go to first today and encourage?

quiz.q: What was the name of the place where Saul nearly caught David and then turned back?
quiz.explain: Because Saul turned back at the news that the Philistines had invaded, the place was called Sela-hammahlekoth (1 Sam 23:27–28).

events.title: The Robe in the Cave at En-gedi
events.subtitle: A hand in the cave that cut a robe instead of a throat
story: Saul came with three thousand chosen men among the Rocks of the Wild Goats at En-gedi. Beside the sheepfolds along the road there was a cave. Saul went into it alone to relieve himself. Deep inside that very cave, in the darkness, David and his men sat holding their breath.

His men whispered to David, “This is the day the Lord told you about, when he would give your enemy into your hand.” David crept up without a sound and quietly cut off a corner of Saul's robe. But when he came back, his conscience struck him. David said to his men, “May the Lord keep me from laying a hand on my lord, the Lord's anointed.” With those words David held his men back from attacking Saul.

When Saul left the cave, David followed him out and called, “My lord the king!” David bowed with his face to the ground, held up the corner of the robe and said, “Look, my father. I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you.” Saul wept aloud and said, “Is that your voice, my son David? You are more righteous than I.” Saul went home, and David went up to the stronghold. A song from that cave remained: “In the shadow of your wings I take refuge.”

words.text: May the Lord forbid that I should lay a hand on my lord, the Lord's anointed, and harm him.
Look, my father. Look at this corner of your robe in my hand. I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, so know that there is no evil or rebellion in me.
You are more righteous than I. I treated you with evil, but you have repaid me with good.
Now I know that you will surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand.

events.note: En-gedi means “spring of the young goat.” It is an oasis where a spring bubbles up beneath the cliffs west of the Dead Sea, and Nubian ibex still live on its rocky heights. The limestone cliffs nearby are full of caves large and small.
events.reflect: If I get a chance to pay back someone who hurt me, can I hold back?

quiz.q: What did David cut from Saul in the cave at En-gedi?
quiz.explain: David got up and quietly cut off a corner of Saul's robe, and afterward his conscience struck him (1 Sam 24:4–5).

events.title: Nabal and Abigail
events.subtitle: One woman facing four hundred men with swords
story: Samuel had died and all Israel was mourning, while at Carmel the sheep-shearing feast was in full swing. It was the feast of Nabal, a rich man with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. David sent ten young men to greet him courteously and ask for food. Nabal sneered: “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? There are plenty of servants these days running away from their masters.”

When the words reached David, he shouted, “Everyone, strap on your swords!” Four hundred men set out with swords at their sides. Meanwhile one of Nabal's servants ran to his mistress Abigail: “David's men were a wall around us night and day, and our master insulted them.” Abigail hurried. She loaded donkeys with two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, and cakes of raisins and figs, and set out without telling her husband.

When she met David coming down the mountain path, Abigail got off her donkey and bowed to the ground. “Let the blame be on me,” Abigail said. “Don't let my lord carry the burden of having shed blood for nothing.” David answered, “Praise the Lord, who sent you to me today. You have kept me from bloodshed.” About ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died. David took Abigail as his wife.

words.text: Praise the Lord, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me. Blessed be your good sense. Today you have kept me from shedding blood.
The Lord will surely build a lasting house for my lord, because my lord fights the Lord's battles, and no evil will be found in you as long as you live.
Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? There are plenty of servants these days running away from their masters.

events.note: This Carmel is not Mount Carmel by the sea but a town in Judah near Maon, south of Hebron. Sheep-shearing time was a season of feasting and generous sharing. “Nabal” means “fool” in Hebrew.
events.reflect: When anger flares up, do I listen to the person trying to stop me?

quiz.q: When did Nabal die after Abigail met David?
quiz.explain: The next morning, sober again, Nabal heard what his wife told him and his body went stiff as stone. About ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died (1 Sam 25:37–38).

events.title: The Spear and Water Jug of Sleeping Saul
events.subtitle: Two men walking through a camp sunk in deep sleep
story: Once again the Ziphites told Saul where David was hiding. Saul led three thousand chosen men and camped beside the road on the hill of Hachilah. That night David looked down on the camp from the hill. Saul lay in the middle, with Abner the commander and the soldiers lying around him. David asked the men beside him, “Who will go down with me into that camp?” Abishai, Joab's brother, stepped forward: “I'll go with you.”

The two walked in among the sleeping men. Saul's spear was stuck in the ground at his head. Abishai whispered, “Let me pin him to the ground with this spear in one stroke. I won't need a second.” David stopped him: “Who can lay a hand on the Lord's anointed and be guiltless? Just take the spear and the water jug, and let's go.” The Lord had sent a deep sleep on them, and no one saw or woke up.

David stood far off on the top of the hill across the way and shouted, “Abner, why didn't you guard your master? Look where the king's spear and water jug are!” Saul recognized David's voice and said, “I have sinned. Come back, my son David.” David told him to send someone for the spear, and went his own way. It was the last time the two would face each other. In the wilderness David sang, “In a dry land my soul thirsts for you.”

words.text: Don't kill him. Who can lay a hand on the Lord's anointed and still claim to be guiltless?
Just as I valued the king's life today, may the Lord value my life and rescue me from every trouble.
I have sinned. Come back, my son David. Because you valued my life today, I will never harm you again. I have truly been a fool.
Today God has given your enemy into your hands. Let me pin him to the ground with the spear in one stroke. I won't need a second.

events.note: This was the last time Saul and David met face to face in life. Abishai was the son of David's sister Zeruiah and the brother of Joab. The heading of Psalm 63 says David wrote it when he was in the wilderness of Judah.
events.reflect: When the same temptation comes again, can I make the choice of faith?

quiz.q: What did David take from beside the head of the sleeping Saul?
quiz.explain: David took the spear and the water jug from beside Saul's head, and no one woke, because the Lord had sent a deep sleep on them (1 Sam 26:12).

events.title: The Day Ziklag Burned
events.subtitle: Finding strength again when there was no strength left to weep
story: David thought to himself, “One of these days I will die at Saul's hand.” He took his six hundred men and their families and put himself in the hands of Achish, king of Gath, in the land of the Philistines. Achish gave him Ziklag. A year and four months passed there. Then one day, sent back from the Philistine camp, they walked three days to get home and found nothing but smoke rising. The Amalekites had burned the town and carried off all the wives and children.

David and his men wept aloud, until they had no strength left to weep. David's two wives had been taken too. The men who had lost their children talked of stoning David. David was in deep distress. But David found strength in the Lord his God. He had Abiathar bring the ephod and asked the Lord. The Lord answered, “Pursue them. You will surely overtake them and surely recover everything.”

At the brook Besor two hundred exhausted men stayed behind while four hundred pursued. In a field they found an Egyptian young man who had not eaten for three days; they fed him, and he showed them the way. David struck the Amalekites in the middle of their feasting and recovered everything. Nothing was missing, not the smallest thing, not a single child. Some of the men grumbled, “The ones who didn't come with us get no share.” David said, “The one who went into battle and the one who stayed with the baggage get the same share.”

words.text: Pursue them. You will surely overtake them, and you will surely recover everything.
My brothers, you must not do that with what the Lord has given us. The Lord has protected us and given into our hands the band that attacked us.
The share of the one who went down into battle is the same as the share of the one who stayed with the baggage. All must share alike.
One of these days I will die at Saul's hand. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines.

events.note: Ziklag was a town in the western Negev that, after Achish gave it to David, belonged to the kings of Judah (1 Sam 27:6). David sent part of the recovered plunder as gifts to the elders of Judah, and sharing the spoils equally became a rule in Israel.
events.reflect: When everything seems to have collapsed, where do I find strength?

quiz.q: How many of David's men were too exhausted to go on and stayed at the brook Besor?
quiz.explain: Of David's six hundred men, two hundred who were exhausted stayed at the brook Besor, and David pursued with four hundred (1 Sam 30:9–10).

events.title: Grief over Gilboa
events.subtitle: The Song of the Bow for a fallen king and a friend
story: The slopes of Mount Gilboa were covered with the bodies of Israel's soldiers. Saul's three sons, Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua, had fallen, and Saul himself was badly wounded by the archers. Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through.” The armor-bearer was too afraid. Saul fell on his own sword. The next day the Philistines hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.

When the warriors of Jabesh-gilead heard, they walked all night and took the bodies of Saul and his sons down from the wall. They buried the bones under the tamarisk tree and fasted seven days. Around that time a young Amalekite came to David at Ziklag, his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He claimed he had killed Saul and held out the crown and the armband. David tore his clothes and wept and fasted until evening.

Then David composed a song and had it taught to the people of Judah. In it, the song called the Bow, David wept: “Your glory, Israel, lies slain on the heights. How the mighty have fallen! Do not tell it in Gath. Mountains of Gilboa, let no dew or rain fall on you. Saul and Jonathan were not parted in life or in death. My brother Jonathan, my heart is torn for you.”

words.text: Your glory, Israel, lies slain on the heights. Oh, how the mighty have fallen!
My brother Jonathan, my heart aches for you. You were so dear to me. Your love for me was more wonderful than the love of women.
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and dear in life, were not parted even in death. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions.
Draw your sword and run me through, so that these uncircumcised men do not come and run me through and make sport of me.

events.note: The Song of the Bow is said to have been written in the Book of Jashar (2 Sam 1:18). Jabesh-gilead was the town Saul first rescued from the Ammonites after he became king (1 Sam 11).
events.reflect: When someone who hated me falls, am I glad or am I grieved?

quiz.q: Who walked all night to take down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall?
quiz.explain: When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard the news, their warriors walked all night, took the bodies from the wall of Beth-shan, buried them at Jabesh and fasted seven days (1 Sam 31:11–13).

events.title: King in Hebron
events.subtitle: The first seat of the man who left the wilderness
story: The news that Saul had fallen on Gilboa reached Ziklag. The throne was empty, but David did not rush. First he asked the Lord, “Shall I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” The Lord said, “Go up.” David asked again, “Where shall I go?” The Lord answered, “To Hebron.” David led his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, along with the men who were with him and their families, up the mountain road and settled in Hebron.

The people of Judah streamed into Hebron and anointed David. The man who had wandered the wilderness was now king over the house of Judah. Then word came to the king that it was the people of Jabesh-gilead, across the Jordan, who had buried Saul. David sent messengers to them: “You showed loyalty to your lord Saul. May the Lord bless you for it. I too will show you kindness.”

After that came a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. When the fighting was over, all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron. The elders said, “We are your own flesh and bone. Even when Saul was king, it was you who led Israel out and brought them in.” David made a covenant with them before the Lord, and the elders anointed him king over all Israel. He had reigned over Judah alone in Hebron for seven and a half years.

words.text: Go up. Go to Hebron.
You showed loyalty to your lord Saul by burying him. May the Lord bless you and show you his steadfast love and faithfulness.
We are your own flesh and bone. The Lord said to you, You will shepherd my people Israel and be their leader.

events.note: Hebron is an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, home to the cave of Machpelah where Abraham lived and was buried. David ruled Judah here for seven and a half years, then moved to Jerusalem and ruled all Israel for thirty-three years.
events.reflect: Even when the waiting drags on, do I ask God instead of trying to hurry things myself?

quiz.q: How old was David when he first became king?
quiz.explain: David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years (2 Sam 5:4).

events.title: The Fortress of Zion
events.subtitle: The city no one could get into
story: David and his soldiers left Hebron and stood before the city of the Jebusites. On a narrow ridge ringed on three sides by deep valleys, the fortress of Zion held firm. From the top of the wall the Jebusites jeered, “You will never get in here. Even the blind and the lame could drive you off.” It was their way of saying David would never set foot in the city.

That day David told his soldiers, “Whoever would strike the Jebusites, go up by the water shaft.” And the city no one could get into fell. David captured the fortress of Zion and went to live there. People called it the City of David. David built the city up all around, from the Millo inward. Because the Lord God of hosts was with him, David grew stronger and stronger.

From Tyre on the northern coast, King Hiram sent envoys. Cedar timber came with them, and carpenters and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David. As the sound of hammers echoed through the fortress, David came to understand that the Lord had firmly established him as king over Israel, and that he had raised up the kingdom not for David's sake alone but for the sake of his people Israel.

words.text: Whoever would strike the Jebusites, go up by the water shaft and strike them.
You will never get in here. Even the blind and the lame could drive you away.

events.note: The City of David lay south of today's Old City of Jerusalem, on a narrow ridge above the Kidron Valley. Some think the vertical shaft once used to draw water up into the city was the water shaft David's men climbed, but this is not certain.
events.reflect: When people say it's impossible, who do I look to?

quiz.q: Which king sent David cedar, carpenters and stonemasons to build his palace?
quiz.explain: Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys with cedar, carpenters and stonemasons, and they built David's palace (2 Sam 5:11).

events.title: Uzzah and the Ark That Stopped
events.subtitle: The threshing floor where a joyful procession halted
story: The sound of lyres and harps, tambourines and cymbals filled the mountain road. David gathered thirty thousand chosen men and went up to Baale-judah to bring back the ark of God, which had stayed a long time in the house of Abinadab. The ark was set on a new cart, and Abinadab's sons Uzzah and Ahio drove it. Ahio walked in front of the ark, and David and all Israel celebrated before the Lord with all their might.

When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, the oxen stumbled and the cart lurched. Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God. At that moment the Lord's anger blazed against Uzzah. God struck him down for his error, and Uzzah died there beside the ark. The music stopped dead. David was angry because the Lord had struck Uzzah, and from that day the place was called Perez-uzzah, the place where Uzzah was struck.

When the anger passed, fear came. David said, “How can the ark of the Lord ever come to me?” He gave up his plan to bring the ark into the City of David and took it instead to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. The ark stayed in that house for three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and his whole household.

words.text: How can the ark of the Lord ever come to me?
The Kohathites are to come and carry the holy things, but they must not touch what is holy, or they will die.
While the ark of the Lord stayed in the house of Obed-edom for three months, the Lord blessed Obed-edom and his whole household.

events.note: The law required the ark to be carried not on a cart but on the shoulders of the Levite clan of Kohath, with poles slid through its rings. After its return from the Philistines, the ark had stayed more than twenty years in the house of Abinadab at Kiriath-jearim.
events.reflect: Am I taking God's word lightly because my intentions are good?

quiz.q: How long did the ark of God stay in the house of Obed-edom?
quiz.explain: The ark of the Lord stayed in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the Lord blessed his household (2 Sam 6:11).

events.title: The Ark Comes Up with Dancing
events.subtitle: A king dancing with all his might
story: Word reached the king that the Lord had blessed the house of Obed-edom. David set out again and brought the ark up with joy. This time it was not on a cart; people carried it. When they had taken six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf. Then, wearing a linen ephod, he danced before the Lord with all his might. Shouts and the blast of trumpets rang through every street of the City of David.

Just then David's wife Michal, Saul's daughter, looked out of a window. She saw the king leaping and dancing before the Lord, and in her heart she despised him. The ark was set in its place inside the tent David had pitched. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings and blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts. Then he gave every man and woman a loaf of bread, a portion of meat and a cake of raisins.

When David came home to bless his household, Michal came out to meet him with a sneer: “How glorious the king of Israel was today, throwing off all dignity before the eyes of his servants' slave girls!” David answered, “It was before the Lord that I danced. Before the one who chose me over your father, I will celebrate. I will make myself even lower than this.” Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no children to the day of her death.

words.text: It was before the Lord that I danced. Before the Lord, who chose me over your father and all his house and made me leader of Israel, I will celebrate.
I will become even lower than this, and humble in my own eyes. But by those slave girls you spoke of, I will be held in honor.
How glorious the king of Israel was today, throwing off his dignity like some vulgar fellow before the eyes of his servants' slave girls!

events.note: The ephod was a short garment worn by priests. That the king wore a linen ephod rather than royal robes is read as a sign that he stood there as a worshiper. This time, as the law required, people carried the ark on their shoulders.
events.reflect: Do I value joy before God more than how people see me?

quiz.q: After how many steps by those carrying the ark did David offer a sacrifice?
quiz.explain: When those carrying the ark had gone six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf (2 Sam 6:13).

events.title: The Promise of an Everlasting House
events.subtitle: A house given to the king who wanted to build one
story: Evening light filtered between the cedar pillars of the palace. The Lord had given David rest from his enemies all around, and at last he could rest. David said to the prophet Nathan, “Look, I live in a house of cedar, while the ark of God stays under curtains.” Nathan answered, “Do whatever is in your heart. The Lord is with you.” But that night the word of the Lord came to Nathan.

The Lord said, “Go and tell my servant David: Are you the one to build me a house? From the day I brought Israel out of Egypt, I have moved about in a tent. I took you from following the flock and made you leader of my people. Now I will build a house for you. A son from your own body will build a house for my name. Your house and your throne will be established forever.”

Nathan went back and passed on the word exactly as it was given. David went in, sat before the Lord and prayed, “Lord God, who am I, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far? And as if this were not enough in your eyes, you have spoken about your servant's house far into the future.” The king who wanted to build God a house had instead been promised a house that would last forever, and he sat a long while before it.

words.text: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, and made you leader over my people Israel.
Your house and your kingdom will stand firm before me forever, and your throne will be established forever.
Lord God, who am I, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?
Go and do everything that is in your heart. The Lord is with you.

events.note: The Hebrew word bayit means “house,” but can also mean a dynasty or a temple. This promise that an everlasting king would come from David's house became the root of Israel's hope for the Messiah, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David.
events.reflect: Before thinking about what to give God, do I remember the grace I have received?

quiz.q: Which prophet brought David the Lord's word about an everlasting house?
quiz.explain: That night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, and Nathan told David all these words (2 Sam 7:4, 17).

events.title: Mephibosheth's Place at the Table
events.subtitle: A man who called himself a dead dog, treated like a prince
story: One day, when the noise of war had died down, David asked his officials, “Is there anyone still left from the house of Saul? I want to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake.” Ziba, who had been a servant in Saul's house, was summoned. Ziba said, “There is still a son of Jonathan. He is lame in both feet.” He was living across the Jordan in Lo-debar, in the house of Machir. David sent for him at once.

The man limped in and fell face down before the king. David called him: “Mephibosheth.” Trembling, Mephibosheth answered, “Your servant is here.” The king said, “Don't be afraid. For the sake of your father Jonathan I will surely show you kindness. I will give you back all the land of Saul, and you will always eat at my table.” Mephibosheth bowed down again. “Why would you look on a dead dog like me?”

The king called Ziba, put Saul's land in his charge, and had him farm it so its harvest would feed his master's household. Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. From that day Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem and always ate at the king's table like one of the king's sons. He had a young son named Mica. Hidden under the table, his two feet were still lame.

words.text: Don't be afraid. For the sake of your father Jonathan I will surely show you kindness. You will always eat at my table.
Is there anyone still left from the house of Saul? I want to show him kindness for Jonathan's sake.
What is your servant, that you should look on a dead dog like me?

events.note: When Mephibosheth was five, the news came that Saul and Jonathan were dead; his nurse picked him up and fled in haste, dropped him, and he became lame in both feet. In an age when new kings wiped out the descendants of the old royal house, David kept his covenant with Jonathan.
events.reflect: Can I make room for others in the place I received by grace?

quiz.q: Where was Mephibosheth living before David sent for him?
quiz.explain: Mephibosheth was in the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar (2 Sam 9:4).

events.title: The Valley of Salt
events.subtitle: The Lord who gave victory wherever he went
story: After that David's army went out in every direction. To the west he struck the Philistines and subdued them; to the east he struck Moab and made them pay tribute. To the north he defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, who was on his way to restore his power toward the Euphrates. The Arameans of Damascus came to help, but they too were broken. The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.

The gold shields carried by Hadadezer's officers were brought to Jerusalem, along with a great amount of bronze taken from his towns. Toi king of Hamath sent his son Joram to greet David, with gifts of silver, gold and bronze vessels. David did not keep them for himself. Together with the silver and gold taken from the nations he had conquered, he dedicated it all to the Lord.

In the Valley of Salt, south below the Dead Sea, David struck down eighteen thousand Edomites, and his name became widely known. David reigned over all Israel and did what was just and right for all his people. Joab was over the army, and Zadok and Ahimelech over the sacrifices. In those days David sang, “Human help is worthless; with God we will fight bravely.”

words.text: The Lord gave David victory wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel and did what was just and right for all his people.
I have been with you wherever you went, and I have cut off all your enemies before you. Now I will make your name great.

events.note: The Valley of Salt is thought to be the salty land south of the Dead Sea, between Judah and Edom. The heading of Psalm 60 remembers the time when Joab, on his return, struck down the Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
events.reflect: Before I boast about what I have done, do I thank God?

quiz.q: Where did David strike down eighteen thousand Edomites?
quiz.explain: David struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and made a name for himself when he returned (2 Sam 8:13).

events.title: On the Roof
events.subtitle: The king who did not go to war
story: Spring came, the time when kings go out to battle. David sent Joab and the whole army of Israel to besiege Rabbah of the Ammonites. But the king himself stayed in Jerusalem. One evening, getting up from his afternoon rest, David was walking on the palace roof when he saw a woman. He sent someone to find out who she was: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. David had her brought to him, and he sinned with another man's wife.

Some time later Bathsheba sent word to the king: “I am pregnant.” David called Uriah back from the battlefield. He asked how the war was going, then told him to go home and rest. But Uriah slept at the palace door with the servants. When the king asked him why, Uriah answered, “The ark and Israel and Judah are staying in tents, and my master Joab is camped in the open field. How could I go home?” Even when the king got him drunk, he would not go home.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it in Uriah's own hand. The letter said: “Put Uriah where the fighting is fiercest, then pull back from him so that he is struck down and dies.” Joab did so, and Uriah died. To the messenger who brought the news the king said, “Tell Joab not to let this trouble him. The sword devours one as well as another.” When the mourning was over, David took Bathsheba as his wife. But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.

words.text: Put Uriah in the front line where the fighting is fiercest, then pull back from him so that he is struck down and dies.
The ark and Israel and Judah are staying in tents, and my master and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How could I go home to eat and drink?
Don't let this trouble you. The sword devours one as well as another.
But what David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.

events.note: Uriah was a Hittite, yet his name is listed among David's thirty-seven greatest warriors. Rabbah was the royal city of Ammon, on the site of Amman, today's capital of Jordan.
events.reflect: Am I letting small greed go unchecked until it leads to greater sin?

quiz.q: Who carried the letter telling Joab to have Uriah killed?
quiz.explain: David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah (2 Sam 11:14).

events.title: You Are the Man
events.subtitle: The king who grew angry at someone else's story
story: The Lord sent the prophet Nathan to David. Standing before the king, Nathan told a story. “There were two men in a certain town, one rich and one poor. The rich man had a great many sheep and cattle, but the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb he had bought and raised. It was like a daughter to him, sleeping in his arms. When a traveler came, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb to serve his guest.”

David burned with anger and shouted, “As surely as the Lord lives, the man who did this deserves to die! He must pay for that lamb four times over.” Nathan looked the king straight in the eye and said, “You are the man.” Then Nathan delivered the word of the Lord: “I made you king. Why have you despised my word, struck down Uriah with the sword and taken his wife?” David said, as if collapsing, “I have sinned against the Lord.”

Nathan answered, “The Lord has taken away your sin. You will not die. But the child who has been born will die.” When the child fell ill, David lay on the ground all night and fasted, and on the seventh day the child died. David got up, washed, and went into the house of the Lord to worship. Later, when Solomon was born, the Lord had him named Jedidiah. In those days David sang, “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”

words.text: Why have you despised my word and done evil in my sight? You struck down Uriah with the sword and took his wife.
I have sinned against the Lord.
You are the man.
While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, thinking the Lord might have mercy. Now that the child is dead, I will go to him, but he will not come back to me.

events.note: The heading of Psalm 51 says David wrote this song when the prophet Nathan came to him after he had sinned with Bathsheba. Jedidiah means “beloved of the Lord.”
events.reflect: Do I see others' wrongs clearly while turning away from my own sin?

quiz.q: What name did the Lord give Solomon through Nathan?
quiz.explain: The Lord loved Solomon and sent Nathan to name him Jedidiah (2 Sam 12:24–25).

events.title: Absalom's Rebellion
events.subtitle: Hearts stolen at the city gate
story: Early in the morning Prince Absalom stood beside the road to the gate of Jerusalem. Behind him were chariots and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him. Whenever he saw someone coming to the king with a lawsuit, Absalom called him over first. “What town are you from?” When the man named his tribe, Absalom would say, “Your case is good and right. But there is no one from the king to hear you. If only someone would make me judge in the land!”

If anyone came near to bow down to him, Absalom would reach out, take hold of him and kiss him. He did this to every Israelite who came to the king for judgment. And so Absalom stole the hearts of the people of Israel. When four years had passed, Absalom said to his father David, “While I was living in exile in Geshur, I made a vow: if the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the Lord. Let me go to Hebron and fulfill that vow.”

Knowing nothing, the king said, “Go in peace.” Absalom went down to Hebron, where his father had first become king. Then he sent secret messengers to all the tribes of Israel: “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, shout, Absalom has become king in Hebron!” Two hundred men invited from Jerusalem went along, knowing nothing at all. While offering sacrifices, Absalom even sent for David's counselor Ahithophel. The conspiracy grew stronger and stronger.

words.text: Go in peace.
If only someone would make me judge in the land! Then anyone with a lawsuit could come to me, and I would see that he got justice.
When you hear the sound of the trumpet, shout: Absalom has become king in Hebron!

events.note: The Hebrew manuscripts give the period as forty years, but it is often read as four years, following the ancient translations. Hebron was where David first became king and where Absalom was born.
events.reflect: Am I losing my sincerity because I want to win people over?

quiz.q: Which of David's counselors did Absalom send for while offering sacrifices in Hebron?
quiz.explain: While offering sacrifices, Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his town of Giloh (2 Sam 15:12).

events.title: Barefoot up the Mount of Olives
events.subtitle: A road climbed barefoot in tears, steps still entrusted to the Lord
story: A messenger rushed into the palace, gasping for breath: “The hearts of Israel have gone over to Absalom.” Absalom, David's own son, had rebelled against his father. David said to his officials, “Get up, we must flee. If we don't hurry, Absalom will put this city to the sword.” The king left the city with his whole household. When the king told Ittai, a commander who had come from Gath of the Philistines, to go back, Ittai answered, “Whether for death or for life, wherever the king is, there I will be.”

The whole land wept aloud. The king crossed the Kidron brook and walked toward the wilderness. The priest Zadok and the Levites followed, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. David said to Zadok, “Carry the ark back into the city. If I find favor in the Lord's eyes, he will bring me back and let me see it again. But if he takes no pleasure in me, here I am; let him do with me as seems good to him.”

David climbed the slope of the Mount of Olives weeping, his head covered and his feet bare. All the people with him covered their heads and wept as well. Then bad news came: even Ahithophel, the king's wise counselor, had sided with Absalom. David prayed, “Lord, turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness.” When he reached the summit where God was worshiped, his friend Hushai came to meet the king, his robe torn and dust on his head. Hushai was the answer God sent to that prayer.

words.text: If I find favor with the Lord, he will bring me back and let me see the ark and the place where he dwells. But if he takes no pleasure in me, here I am; let him do with me as seems good to him.
Lord, turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness.
As surely as the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever the king may be, whether for death or for life, there I will be too.

events.note: The Kidron brook runs through the valley between the eastern wall of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, and it flows only in the rainy season. About a thousand years later, on the night he was arrested, Jesus too crossed this brook to a garden on the slopes of the Mount of Olives.
events.reflect: When I must let go of what I've been holding on to, can I trust God?

quiz.q: Which man from Gath told the fleeing David, “Whether for death or for life, wherever the king is, there I will be”?
quiz.explain: Ittai the Gittite, even when the king told him to go back, answered that he would be wherever the king was, whether for death or for life (2 Sam 15:19–21). Hushai went back to the city to defeat Ahithophel's counsel (2 Sam 15:32–34).

events.title: Shimei's Stones
events.subtitle: A king who put away the sword under stones and curses
story: As they reached Bahurim, a man came down from the hillside. It was Shimei son of Gera, from the family of Saul. Shimei threw stones at the king and his officials and shouted, “Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! You took the place of the house of Saul, and now the Lord is paying you back for that blood. The kingdom has been handed over to your son Absalom.” Warriors with swords at their sides stood all around the king.

Abishai, Joab's brother, gripped the hilt of his sword. “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head.” David shook his head. “What do you and I have in common, you sons of Zeruiah? If the Lord told him to curse David, who can blame him? My own son, my flesh and blood, is after my life. How much more this Benjamite? Leave him alone.”

David added in a low voice, “Perhaps the Lord will see my distress and repay me with good instead of the curses I hear today.” David and his men went on along the road. Shimei kept pace with them along the hillside opposite, cursing as he went, throwing stones and flinging dust. The king never raised his sword. Worn out, the people could only catch their breath when they reached a place to rest.

words.text: My own son, my flesh and blood, is after my life. How much more this Benjamite! Leave him alone. The Lord has told him to do this.
Perhaps the Lord will see my distress and repay me with good in place of the curses he pours on me today.
Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head.
Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!

events.note: Bahurim is thought to have been a Benjamite village beyond the Mount of Olives, on the road down from Jerusalem to the Jordan Valley. It was also the village where Michal's husband Paltiel, who had followed her weeping, turned back.
events.reflect: Faced with unfair blame, can I leave it with God instead of reacting on impulse?

quiz.q: From whose family was Shimei, who threw stones at David and cursed him?
quiz.explain: Shimei was the son of Gera, a relative of Saul's family, and he cursed David, calling him a man who had shed the blood of Saul's house (2 Sam 16:5–8).

events.title: Mahanaim
events.subtitle: A table spread in a strange land for a king in flight
story: After crossing the Jordan, David came to Mahanaim, a town in Gilead. Absalom followed, crossing the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Absalom made Amasa, Joab's cousin, commander of the army in Joab's place, and camped in the land of Gilead. The armies of father and son glared at each other in the same land. The king's people, who had come through the wilderness, were exhausted and hungry.

Just then donkeys loaded with goods came in through the town gate. They belonged to Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah, the Ammonite city; Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar; and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim. They unloaded beds, basins and clay pots. After them came wheat and barley, flour and roasted grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds, sheep, and cheese from the herd.

The three men said to the king, “The people must be hungry, tired and thirsty from the wilderness.” Machir was the man who had taken Saul's grandson Mephibosheth into his home, and Shobi came from the very Ammonite capital David had brought down. Driven out by his own son, the king sat before a table spread for him in a strange land. Only then did the weary people eat and drink.

words.text: The people must be hungry, tired and thirsty from the wilderness.
They brought beds, basins and clay pots, wheat, barley and flour, roasted grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds, sheep and cheese, for David and the people with him to eat.

events.note: Mahanaim means “two camps,” the name Jacob gave the place when he met the angels of God. It was also where Saul's son Ish-bosheth was made king after Saul's death.
events.reflect: What can I give for someone who is weary and struggling?

quiz.q: Which of these did NOT bring food to David at Mahanaim?
quiz.explain: Shobi of Rabbah, Machir of Lo-debar and Barzillai of Rogelim brought household goods and food (2 Sam 17:27–29). Ahithophel was the counselor who had sided with Absalom (2 Sam 15:12).

events.title: The Oak in the Forest of Ephraim
events.subtitle: A prince hanging between heaven and earth
story: Beside the gate of Mahanaim, David divided his troops into three and put them under Joab, Abishai and Ittai the Gittite. When the king said he would go out with them, the people stopped him: “You are worth ten thousand of us. Stay in the city and help us from there.” As the army marched out of the gate by hundreds and by thousands, the king gave the three commanders an order in everyone's hearing: “For my sake, deal gently with the young man Absalom.”

The battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim. The Israelite army that followed Absalom collapsed before David's men, and twenty thousand fell that day. The fighting spread over the whole countryside, and the forest swallowed more men than the sword. Absalom was riding a mule, and as it passed under the tangled branches of a great oak, his head caught fast. The mule kept going, and Absalom was left hanging between heaven and earth.

A soldier who saw it told Joab. When Joab demanded why he hadn't struck him down, the soldier answered, “Even if you put a thousand shekels of silver in my hand, I would not lay a hand on the king's son.” Joab would hear no more. He took three small spears and thrust them into the heart of Absalom, who was still alive, and ten of Joab's men finished him off. Joab blew the trumpet and stopped the battle. They threw Absalom into a pit in the forest and piled a great heap of stones over him.

words.text: For my sake, deal gently with the young man Absalom.
You must not go out. You are worth ten thousand of us. It is better for you to stay in the city and help us from there.
Even if a thousand shekels of silver were put in my hand, I would not lay a hand on the king's son. The king gave you that order in the hearing of us all.

events.note: While he was alive, Absalom set up a pillar bearing his own name in the King's Valley, saying he had no son to carry on his name. The tomb in the Kidron Valley known today as “Absalom's Monument” was built in a much later age.
events.reflect: Can I correct someone who has done wrong without losing compassion?

quiz.q: What did Joab thrust into Absalom as he hung in the oak?
quiz.explain: Joab took three small spears and thrust them into the heart of Absalom, who was still alive and hanging in the oak, and ten young men who carried Joab's armor struck him and killed him (2 Sam 18:14–15).

events.title: O My Son Absalom
events.subtitle: A father's cry that broke out on the day of victory
story: When the fighting was over, Ahimaaz son of the priest Zadok begged Joab, “Let me run and take the good news to the king.” Joab said not today, and sent a Cushite instead. It was the day the king's son had died. But when Ahimaaz kept on begging, Joab at last gave in. Ahimaaz ran by way of the Jordan plain and overtook the Cushite, who had set out first.

David was sitting between the two gates, waiting. The watchman on the wall called out, “A man is running this way. There's another one behind him. The first one runs like Ahimaaz.” Ahimaaz bowed down and announced the victory, but the king asked only one thing: “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz gave a vague answer. The Cushite arrived after him and said, “May all the king's enemies end up like that young man.”

The king shook and went up to the room above the gate, crying out, “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you!” That day the victory turned into weeping, and the soldiers crept back into the city like men who had fled from battle. Joab came in and confronted the king: “If you don't go out now and reassure your men, not one of them will be left with you tonight.” The king got up and took his seat in the gate.

words.text: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you! O Absalom, my son, my son!
Is the young man Absalom safe?
May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up to harm you, be like that young man.
You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. Now get up, go out and encourage your men.

events.note: David's cry “O my son Absalom” is the first verse of chapter 19 in the Hebrew Bible. The city gate was where courts and councils met, so the king taking his seat in the gate meant he was standing before his people once more.
events.reflect: Can I pray even for someone who has hurt me?

quiz.q: Who reached David first after the battle?
quiz.explain: The Cushite set out first, but Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and overtook him (2 Sam 18:21–23). Absalom's death was made known by the words of the Cushite, who came after him (2 Sam 18:32).

events.title: The Threshing Floor of Araunah
events.subtitle: I will not offer a sacrifice that costs me nothing
story: At a time when the Lord's anger burned against Israel again, David ordered Joab, “Go through all Israel and count the people.” Joab objected: “Why does the king want to do this?” But the king's word prevailed. After nine months and twenty days the numbers came in: eight hundred thousand fighting men in Israel, five hundred thousand in Judah. Faced with those numbers, David's conscience struck him. David said to the Lord, “I have sinned greatly.”

The next morning the prophet Gad came and delivered the word of the Lord: “Choose one: famine, three months of fleeing from your enemies, or three days of plague.” David answered, “Let me fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercy is great, and not into human hands.” A plague swept through the land, and seventy thousand died from Dan to Beersheba. When the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem, the Lord relented and said to the angel, “Enough. Withdraw your hand.”

At that moment the angel was standing by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. When David saw the angel, he cried out to the Lord, “I am the one who sinned. What have these sheep done?” As Gad had told him, David went up there, and Araunah bowed low and offered to give him the threshing floor and the oxen for nothing. David shook his head: “I will not offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” David bought the threshing floor for fifty shekels of silver and built an altar, and the plague stopped.

words.text: Enough. Withdraw your hand.
I am the one who has sinned. I am the one who did wrong. These sheep, what have they done? Let your hand fall on me and on my father's house.
No, I insist on paying for it. I will not offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God that cost me nothing.
Let my lord the king take whatever he thinks best and offer it. May the Lord your God accept you with favor.

events.note: Chronicles records that this threshing floor was on Mount Moriah and that Solomon built the temple on that very spot. It is thought to be the same land of Moriah where Abraham went up to offer Isaac.
events.reflect: In what I give to God, am I putting my own comfort and benefit first?

quiz.q: What did David pay Araunah for the threshing floor and the oxen?
quiz.explain: Saying he would not offer burnt offerings that cost him nothing, David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver (2 Sam 24:24). The six hundred shekels of gold in 1 Chronicles 21:25 is recorded as the price of the whole site.
